entry.title: SurrealDB: One Rust Binary for Documents, Graphs, and Vectors

link.title: SurrealDB: One Rust Binary for Documents, Graphs, and Vectors

entry.content:
If you have ever built an AI-flavored application, you know the drill: documents go into a document store, the relationship graph goes into a graph database, embeddings go into a dedicated vector engine such as Qdrant or Milvus, and then you spend weeks wiring four systems together, keeping them consistent, and paying four infrastructure bills. Multi-model databases attack this sprawl at the root. Instead of bolting a JSON column onto a relational engine or gluing a vector index onto a key-value cache, they commit to one storage core that treats documents, graph edges, and high-dimensional vectors as first-class citizens.

SurrealDB is one of the most ambitious entries in this category. It is written entirely in Rust, ships as a single binary, and — according to its README — unifies “document, graph, relational, time-series, geospatial and key-value data types with powerful search and retrieval functionalities (full-text, vector, hybrid)” plus real-time capabilities. It can run embedded in your process, compiled to WebAssembly for the browser, on the edge, as a self-hosted node, or as a distributed cluster. SurrealDB even doubles as an API backend: row-level permissions, scope-based user signup, and live queries that push changes to clients are built in, so the traditional backend service between your app and the database can shrink or disappear. The core database code is licensed under the Business Source License 1.1, with SDKs and libraries under Apache 2.0 or MIT.

What does that look like inside? In this post we walk the actual source of surrealdb/surrealdb on the main branch (commit 18971ffba781) and trace the path a query takes: from the CLI that starts the server, through the HTTP and WebSocket surfaces, into the SurrealQL parser, the executor, the per-record document engine, and finally the key-value storage layer where RocksDB, SurrealKV, memory, and TiKV live. Two diagrams anchor the tour: an overview of the major layers, and a detailed map of the modules and entry points.

Overview: CLI boots the server, the Axum HTTP router fans out to RPC and SQL endpoints, queries flow through the executor and document engine, and every read and write lands in a pluggable KV backend.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Commands enum, L167 — the Clap-derived subcommand table. Start is described as “Start the database server” and Sql as “Start an SQL REPL in your terminal with pipe support”, so the same binary is both server and client tool.
  • start::init, L212 — server bootstrap. The --bind flag defaults to 127.0.0.1:8000 (see the arg definition, L158), overridable via the SURREAL_BIND environment variable.
  • community_router, L151 — an Axum router that merges the /rpc handler, L38, the /sql handler, L28, /signin, /signup, /key, export/import, GraphQL, and MCP routes into one service.
  • RpcProtocol trait, L95 — the protocol-agnostic JSON-RPC surface. Its execute method matches the wire method and dispatches to typed handlers like query and signin; the Method enum, L3 enumerates them.
  • Datastore, L210 — the central object. Datastore::new, L951 takes a URL such as memory, rocksdb://, surrealkv://, or tikv://127.0.0.1:2379 and builds the engine; Datastore::execute, L3437 parses SurrealQL text and runs it.
  • Executor, L51 — drives each parsed statement through its compute method and collects per-statement results, timings, and observability events.
  • Iterator::process, L1206 — the bridge from scanning to document semantics: for every candidate record it constructs a Document and invokes select, create, update, relate, or delete on it.
  • Transactor, L37 — the transaction facade every backend implements, with TransactionType (Read/Write) and LockType (Pessimistic/Optimistic) chosen per statement.

Detail map: HTTP surface, RPC and auth modules, parser and statement types, the executor with its index planners, the document engine, all four KV backends, and the full-text and vector index subsystems.

One Storage Contract, Many Backends

SurrealDB’s storage design is a classic “KV core, many engines” play — the same philosophy that made Redis successful, but applied to a full database rather than a cache. Everything above the storage layer only ever sees byte keys and byte values inside transactions. The concrete engine is chosen by a URL scheme.

The dispatch happens in the flavour match, L620: memory (with mem accepted as an alias), rocksdb, surrealkv, indxdb (the browser/WASM engine), and tikv for distributed deployments. A nice archaeological detail: the legacy file: scheme was removed, and the code now fails with a targeted message — “The file:// scheme is no longer supported; use rocksdb:// or surrealkv:// instead” — instead of a generic error.

Each backend implements the same transaction contract. The in-memory engine is a compact Datastore struct, L34; the RocksDB engine initializes in rocksdb::Datastore::new, L349 and carries its own background flusher, commit coordinator, memory manager, and garbage collector; SurrealKV — the project’s own disk engine — does the same in surrealkv::Datastore::new, L68. Transactions themselves are expressed in kvs/tr.rs: a Transactor wraps any backend-specific Transactable implementation, exposes get, set, scan, commit, and cancel, and even logs an error if a writeable transaction is dropped without being committed — a small guard that catches real bugs.

The plumbing that assembles a Datastore is worth a glance too: Builder::build_with_path, L195 threads a TransactionBuilder, a live-query broker, capabilities, and index stores into the final struct. The TransactionBuilder trait exists precisely so external crates can plug in custom backends while reusing everything above it.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps installation to one command per platform. On Linux or macOS:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://install.surrealdb.com | sh

On macOS you can alternatively brew install surrealdb/tap/surreal, and on Windows iwr https://windows.surrealdb.com -useb | iex. Docker works too, and the README’s dev-mode example is the fastest way to poke at the system: docker run --rm --pull always --name surrealdb -p 8000:8000 surrealdb/surrealdb:latest start --log info --user root --pass root memory — an in-memory server on port 8000 with root credentials.

Once installed, surreal start boots the server (default bind address 127.0.0.1:8000) and surreal sql drops you into an interactive SurrealQL shell. Then the multi-model part begins. Define a schemafull table with fields, a unique index, and an event, exactly as the README shows:

DEFINE TABLE user SCHEMAFULL;
DEFINE FIELD email ON TABLE user TYPE string ASSERT string::is_email($value);
DEFINE INDEX email ON TABLE user COLUMNS email UNIQUE;
DEFINE EVENT email ON TABLE user WHEN $before.email != $after.email THEN (
    CREATE event SET user = $value, time = time::now(), action = 'email_changed'
);

Graph edges come from RELATE, which the README demonstrates as RELATE user:tobie->write->article:surreal SET time.written = time::now(); — no join tables, no separate graph engine. If you later need analytical workloads that SurrealDB is not aiming for, that is where column-oriented tools like DuckDB or ClickHouse complement rather than replace it.

How a Query Actually Runs

The execution path is a chain of well-separated stages. Text arrives at Datastore::execute, L3437, which first checks session expiry and anonymous-access policy, then calls syn::parse_with_capabilities, L107. The parser — a hand-written lexer and recursive-descent parser under surrealdb/core/src/syn/ — validates the query against the datastore’s capability flags before producing an Ast.

Statements then reach the Executor, L51, whose design the code summarizes in one line: “An executor which relies on the compute methods of the logical expressions.” Each statement type carries its own compute logic. For a SELECT, SelectStatement::compute in select.rs creates a QueryPlanner and an Iterator; the borrowed Statement enum, L38 then matches the statement variant at Iterator::process, L1206 and hands each record to the right document operation.

Index selection lives in two generations of planners. The streaming executor’s Planner, L124 — with its plan method at L528 — turns expressions into physical operator trees, while IndexAnalyzer, L19 produces candidates and select_access_path, L235 chooses between B-tree scans, full-text scans, and KNN scans. The module documentation in exec/index.rs even includes an ASCII diagram of this planner-then-execute split.

The search subsystems are genuine multi-model proof. Full-text search is a real inverted index with BM25 scoring — see FullTextIndex, L151 and its Bm25Params. Vector search ships two independent index families: HnswIndex, L172 and a DiskANN implementation under idx/trees/diskann/, with a bounded top-k helper in KnnPriorityList, L11. You do not need a sidecar vector database for moderate-scale semantic search — the same reasons teams reach for pgvector apply here, minus the PostgreSQL dependency.

Auth, Realtime, and the RPC Surface

The document engine’s per-record lifecycle is where SurrealDB’s “database as API backend” claim gets real. Document::create, L10 reads like a checklist: permission gate, view-table rejection, input computation, record-id generation, table-type check, default fields, schema field processing, create permissions, storage via store_record_data, L10, index maintenance, table references, views, events, live-query fan-out, and changefeeds — before output projection runs. Graph edges follow the same discipline in Document::relate, L11.

Authentication is layered the same way. The HTTP endpoints /signin, L41 and /signup, L39 delegate to the IAM module: iam::signin, L92 verifies access grants at root, namespace, or database level and supports bearer records, while iam::signup, L79 provisions scoped users. Over WebSocket, the server implements the same RpcProtocol trait on Websocket, L717, with explicit begin, commit, and cancel handlers and live-query registration in handle_live, L857. There is even a stdio MCP server subcommand “for AI assistant integration” — SurrealDB is clearly aiming at the agent-tooling ecosystem, not just human developers.

Honest Limits

A few caveats worth knowing before you commit. First, licensing: the core database code is BSL 1.1, not a classic OSS license — fine for most products, but read the terms if you plan to offer SurrealDB itself as a service. Second, storage backends are a moveable feast: file:// is gone, TiKV support depends on build features, and the README’s Docker examples lean on memory or rocksdb, so pick rocksdb:// or surrealkv:// deliberately for persistence. Third, the GraphQL interface is listed in the README as “coming soon”, so HTTP /sql and JSON-RPC over WebSocket are the stable query surfaces today. Fourth, “multi-model” does not mean “best at everything”: heavy analytical scans are still the territory of DuckDB, and extremely large-scale vector workloads may still justify a dedicated engine — SurrealDB gives you the integrated default, not necessarily the extreme-end specialist. Finally, the two vector index families (HNSW and DiskANN) and the enterprise/community split visible in the code (the CommunityComposer versus enterprise brokers in kvs/ds/builder.rs) mean feature availability varies by edition and build flags — verify against the docs for your exact version.

None of these limits are unusual for a system this young and this broad. What is unusual is how coherent the implementation is: one KV contract, one parser, one executor, one document lifecycle — and four storage engines, three index families, and two wire protocols that all slot into the same seams. If your next project needs documents, relationships, and embeddings in one store, SurrealDB deserves a spot on your shortlist next to Redis stack hybrids and Qdrant-backed stacks.

entry.title: Tantivy source tour: how the Rust full-text search engine library works

link.title: Tantivy source tour: how the Rust full-text search engine library works

entry.content:
Most search tutorials stop at the API surface. This one goes the other way: we open the crate itself. Tantivy is a fast full-text search engine library written in Rust — closer in spirit to Apache Lucene than to a turnkey server like Elasticsearch, in the words of its own README. It is the engine underneath Quickwit, and ParadeDB ships it inside Postgres for pg_search. The crate is at version 0.27.0 on the main branch; every file path and line number below was verified against that tree with grep before being linked.

Two diagrams accompany the tour. Both were generated from the actual repository layout rather than from memory, and both are clickable — each node links to the exact source file on GitHub. The first is a high-level pass over the whole system; the second zooms into seven subsystems: schema, core objects, the indexer, storage, querying, the inverted index, and tokenizers. If you have ever wondered what actually happens between add_document and a scored hit list, the answer is a chain of data structures with wonderful Lucene-flavored names: postings, term dictionaries, field norms, fast fields, and the doc store.

A caution before we start: Tantivy is a library, not a service. There is no cluster and no REST endpoint. The interesting complexity is entirely in the on-disk data structures and the commit protocol that keeps readers consistent while writers mutate the index. That is exactly the layer these diagrams try to make visible.

Overview: documents flow from a frozen schema through the multithreaded writer into immutable segment files, while the read side reloads those files into Searcher snapshots. Every node links to its source file on the main branch.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts with SchemaBuilder. You declare fields with typed options — add_text_field at line 163, then build() at line 244 freezes an immutable Schema. Each field becomes a FieldEntry (src/schema/field_entry.rs) carrying a FieldType — text, u64, f64, date, facet, bytes, or JSON.
  • The Index struct pairs that schema with a storage location. create_in_ram (line 444) and open (line 650) are the two ways in; reader() at line 590 and writer() at line 753 hand out the two halves of the system.
  • On the write side, IndexWriter is the only door in. add_document (line 741) routes each document to one of several indexing threads, delete_term (line 694) enqueues a tombstone, and commit (line 678) makes everything visible atomically.
  • Each thread owns a SegmentWriter that buffers a batch in memory: it tokenizes text, fills the in-memory postings, store, fast fields and field norms, and only then seals the batch to disk.
  • At commit time the SegmentManager takes over — it tracks which segments are live, applies queued deletes, and consults LogMergePolicy about when to compact.
  • Merges run in background threads through the IndexMerger, which streams several segments into one while dropping deleted documents along the way.
  • On the read side, IndexReader watches for new commits and searcher() at line 315 vends an immutable Searcher snapshot.
  • Finally, a QueryParser turns title:sea AND body:whale into a query tree, and search() at line 180 pushes every match into a collector such as TopDocs.

The detailed view: 34 code-level nodes across seven subsystems, from the FST-backed term dictionary down to the bitpacked posting blocks.

Why an index is a forest of immutable segments

The single most important design fact in Tantivy is that an index is a collection of small, independent, immutable segments. Each segment is identified by a UUID-based SegmentId and owns its own copy of every data structure. A tiny meta.json records the live segment list plus the schema, and commit swaps that file atomically. SegmentMeta carries the bookkeeping: doc counts, max doc, whether the segment has deletes.

Immutability is what buys the O(1)-memory search the architecture notes promise. Readers never see a half-written segment; they see old files that are still complete or new files that are already complete. The cost shows up in deletes: there is no in-place update. delete_term marks documents dead in a per-segment alive bitset (see src/fastfield/alive_bitset.rs), and the reclaimed space only truly comes back when the IndexMerger rewrites the segment without the tombstoned docs. Every mutating operation gets an incrementing opstamp, which is how the writer serializes concurrent adds, deletes, and commits.

Inside the inverted index

The inverted index is the bread and butter. When a document with the text “Hello, happy tax payer!” arrives, the configured analyzer splits it into tokens — the default tokenizer lowercases and produces [hello, happy, tax, payer] — and the document is registered under terms like text:hello. The term lookup is chained through two structures. First, an FST (finite state transducer) maps Term to a term ordinal in src/termdict/mod.rs. Then a term info store maps that ordinal to a TermInfo, which holds the byte offsets of the posting list inside the .idx file.

Posting lists themselves are blocks of 128 documents: doc ids delta-encoded and bitpacked, term frequencies bitpacked separately, with a variable-int tail for the final partial block. When positions are indexed, a separate .pos file stores token offsets so phrase queries can verify adjacency. The InvertedIndexSerializer writes all of this at seal time; the InvertedIndexReader replays it at query time. Two smaller satellites complete the picture: field norms (src/fieldnorm/writer.rs) store one byte per document — the token count of a field — because the BM25 formula needs it, and fast fields (src/fastfield/writer.rs) are the column-oriented, bitpacked equivalent of Lucene’s doc values, giving you a one-memory-fetch random access by doc id for scoring, filtering, and aggregations.

Scoring and the query machine

Query execution follows a three-trait assembly line. The Query trait is the user-facing tree: QueryParser builds it, BooleanQuery composes sub-queries with Must/Should/MustNot clauses, and TermQuery is the leaf that iterates one term’s posting list. The Weight trait is the per-searcher precomputation — this is where Bm25Weight gathers term and field statistics needed for scoring. Finally the Scorer trait pairs iteration with scoring: it is a cursor over matching doc ids, and boolean queries implement it by merging child cursors.

Underneath everything sits the DocSet trait — a sorted iterator of doc ids, which is what makes intersections and unions cheap. On the consumer side, the Collector trait decides what to do with each (doc, score) pair: TopDocs keeps the top K, while the aggregation collector (src/aggregation/collector.rs) computes histograms, ranges, averages, and stats over fast fields.

From Install to Your First Model

Here is the shortest realistic path to a working index, following the crate’s documented basic search example. Start a fresh project and pull the crate:

cargo add tantivy

Then build a schema, index two documents in memory, and search them. This uses only APIs verified above: Schema::builder, Index::create_in_ram, index.writer, the doc! macro from src/macros.rs, commit, and the reader/searcher pair:

use tantivy::collector::TopDocs;
use tantivy::query::QueryParser;
use tantivy::schema::*;
use tantivy::{doc, Index, TantivyDocument};

fn main() -> tantivy::Result<()> {
    let mut schema_builder = Schema::builder();
    let title = schema_builder.add_text_field("title", TEXT | STORED);
    let body = schema_builder.add_text_field("body", TEXT);
    let schema = schema_builder.build();

    let index = Index::create_in_ram(schema);
    let mut writer = index.writer(50_000_000)?;
    writer.add_document(doc!(
        title => "The Old Man and the Sea",
        body => "He was an old man who fished alone in a skiff.",
    ))?;
    writer.add_document(doc!(
        title => "Of Mice and Men",
        body => "A few miles south of Soledad, the Salinas River drops in close.",
    ))?;
    writer.commit()?;

    let reader = index.reader()?;
    let searcher = reader.searcher();
    let parser = QueryParser::for_index(&index, vec![title, body]);
    for (score, addr) in searcher.search(&parser.parse_query("old man")?, &TopDocs::with_limit(10))? {
        let doc: TantivyDocument = searcher.doc(addr)?;
        println!("{score}: {}", doc.to_json(&schema));
    }
    Ok(())
}

Three habits from the source are worth copying immediately. First, treat commit as the visibility boundary — nothing is searchable before it, as the README’s FAQ states. Second, call reader.reload() if you hold a long-lived reader and want to see later commits; the reload policy can do this automatically on commit. Third, model your delete key explicitly: since Tantivy has no primary id, you pick a field (say, a stored URL or numeric id) and delete_term against it when a document changes.

Storage: Directory trait and the doc store

Everything above touches files through one abstraction, the Directory trait. The crate ships two implementations: MmapDirectory, the default for on-disk indexes whose readers get memory-mapped views (so “loading” an index is essentially just mmapping its files), and RamDirectory for in-memory use. You can implement the trait yourself to put segments anywhere.

The doc store is the row-oriented sibling of the inverted index. StoreWriter compresses each stored document into blocks with LZ4 or Zstd; StoreReader later reconstructs full documents by doc id for result display. The architecture notes are blunt about the cost model: a store fetch walks a skip index and decompresses a block, so it is meant for the top results you will actually render — their rule of thumb is that hitting the store more than a hundred times per query means you are misusing it. Tokenization is pluggable through the TokenizerManager registry, where each named entry produces a TextAnalyzer — a tokenizer chained with filters like lowercasing and stemming.

Honest Limits

Limits stated by the project’s own documentation, not invented here:

  • The relevance score is not configurable. Tantivy uses BM25, the same formula family as Lucene and Elasticsearch’s default similarity, per the architecture document.
  • Distributed search is explicitly out of scope. The README points you to Quickwit for that layer; the crate itself is a single-node engine library.
  • The schema imposes a one-to-one mapping between ingested fields and indexed fields. Wanting one text indexed twice with different analyzers, or indexing a concatenation of several fields, means duplicating or concatenating the fields yourself before feeding them in — the architecture document names this as a current limitation.
  • Updates are batch-shaped by design. Adds and deletes are cheap to express but the index is architected around commits and merges; dynamic per-document mutation is not the design center.
  • There is no primary key or built-in document identity, so update-by-id is your responsibility (delete term, then re-add).
  • The performance numbers floating around — roughly 2x Lucene on their latency benchmark, Wikipedia indexed in about three minutes on the author’s desktop — come from the project’s own README and benchmark page; the README itself warns that your mileage will vary with query and workload.

If this tour landed well, two adjacent reads on this blog: my Elasticsearch architecture tour covers the server-side layer Tantivy deliberately omits, ParadeDB shows what happens when this engine is embedded in Postgres, and for the “search by meaning rather than keyword” side, see FAISS and LanceDB for vector indexes, or Meilisearch for a batteries-included Rust search server.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of Tantivy, the Lucene-inspired Rust full-text search engine library, with architecture diagrams traced through the real code on the main branch.

entry.title: TimescaleDB Source Tour: How Hypertables, Chunk Routing, Columnstore, and Continuous Aggregates Actually Work

link.title: TimescaleDB Source Tour: How Hypertables, Chunk Routing, Columnstore, and Continuous Aggregates Actually Work

entry.content:
TimescaleDB is a PostgreSQL extension for high-performance real-time analytics on time-series and event data, developed by Timescale (now Tiger Data). Unlike a fork of Postgres or a separate storage engine, it is a loadable extension written in C that hooks deeply into the planner, the executor, and the DDL machinery of the database itself. That design choice explains almost everything you see when you open the repository: there is a src/ directory that talks to PostgreSQL core through well-defined hooks, a sql/ directory that ships the extension’s user-visible functions and catalog definitions, and a tsl/ directory that holds the licensed “TSL” features — columnstore compression and continuous aggregates — behind a small cross-module interface.

This post is a source tour of the main branch (version 2.32.0-dev at the time of writing). We rendered two interactive architecture diagrams directly from the source tree: an overview graph that fits on one screen, and a detail graph that separates the extension into eight functional groups. Every symbol mentioned below was located with grep in the actual sources, so the line-number links take you to exact code in the timescale/timescaledb repository on GitHub.

The mental model to keep in mind: a “hypertable” is the user-facing table, but it is backed by many PostgreSQL child tables called chunks, one per time (and optionally space) interval. Writes arrive at the parent table, get translated into a point in a multi-dimensional space, and are routed into the right chunk. Everything else — columnstore compression, continuous aggregates, retention and refresh policies — is machinery layered on top of that single idea.

Overview of the timescale/timescaledb codebase. SQL entry points become hypertable metadata in the catalog; every write is partitioned and routed to a chunk; the planner wraps DML so routing happens at execution time; TSL code adds columnstore compression and continuous aggregates.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The journey starts in SQL: create_hypertable, L21 in sql/ddl_api.sql is the user-facing function that turns an ordinary PostgreSQL table into a hypertable.
  • That SQL wrapper calls into C: ts_hypertable_create, L1576 validates options and drives ts_hypertable_create_internal, L1482, which registers the hypertable in the metadata tables exposed by catalog_get_table, L569.
  • Dimensions come next: ts_dimension_calculate_default_slice, L433 computes the interval boundaries for the time dimension, and ts_dimension_slice_scan_limit, L440 finds which slice covers a given coordinate.
  • On every insert, ts_partitioning_func_apply, L271 maps column values to an int64 coordinate, and ts_chunk_tuple_routing_find_chunk, L72 picks — or creates — the target chunk via ts_chunk_create_for_point, L1665.
  • Before a row lands in a child table, ts_chunk_insert_state_create, L466 builds the per-chunk insert state that carries triggers, indexes, and result relation info.
  • For queries, the planner hook timescaledb_planner, L631 rewrites plans against hypertables, and DML gets wrapped by ts_modify_hypertable_path_create, L797 so that modify_hypertable_exec, L290 can route tuples at execution time.
  • In the licensed tsl/ tree, compress_chunk, L300 rewrites row chunks into compressed columnar batches, while continuous_agg_refresh, L970 incrementally materializes continuous aggregates from invalidation ranges.

Why the Codebase Is Shaped This Way

TimescaleDB cannot patch PostgreSQL itself, so it attaches at every seam the extension API exposes. During library load, _PG_init, L89 installs hooks for planning, DDL, COPY, and executor callbacks, and registers the timescaledb.* GUC settings (for example enable_direct_compress_insert in src/guc.c). Until the user runs CREATE EXTENSION, all of that machinery stays dormant: ts_extension_is_loaded, L285 is the gate checked throughout the code, which is why the extension can sit safely loaded inside any Postgres instance.

Because hooks alone do not give you a clean internal API, the code routes shared state through caches. The generic pinned-cache infrastructure lives in src/cache.c (ts_cache_pin, L122), and the most important user of it is the hypertable cache: ts_hypertable_cache_get_entry, L189 turns a relation OID into a Hypertable object once per transaction and pins it so executor callbacks can reuse it without re-scanning the catalog. Chunk lookups get the same treatment via a hypercube-keyed memo in ts_subspace_store_get, L198, which avoids hitting the chunk catalog table on every routed row.

DDL interception deserves its own mention. A CREATE TABLE ... WITH (tsdb.hypertable) statement, or an ALTER TABLE ... SET (timescaledb.compress), flows through the process-utility hook timescaledb_ddl_command_start, L6593. That single function is one of the largest files in the extension for a reason: every DDL statement that touches a hypertable (dropping chunks, truncating, adding columns) must be translated so that the same operation happens on the right set of child tables and catalog rows.

From Install to Your First Model

The repository README’s quick start is genuinely one-command. With Docker running, the fastest path is:

curl -sL https://tsdb.co/start-local | sh

That script starts a tuned container, exposes PostgreSQL on port 6543, and sets up a persistent volume. If you prefer to do it manually — the README notes this is also the Windows path — the equivalent is:

docker run -d --name timescaledb \
    -p 6543:5432 \
    -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=password \
    timescale/timescaledb-ha:pg18

The timescale/timescaledb-ha:pg18 image ships TimescaleDB pre-installed and pre-loaded. Connect with psql -h localhost -p 6543 -U postgres (password password). If you are using a self-managed PostgreSQL instead of the Docker image, the standard sequence is CREATE EXTENSION timescaledb; after adding shared_preload_libraries = 'timescaledb' — the preload is what lets _PG_init install the hooks described above.

Now create your first data model, straight from the README’s Step 3:

CREATE TABLE sensor_data (
    time TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    sensor_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    temperature DOUBLE PRECISION,
    humidity DOUBLE PRECISION,
    pressure DOUBLE PRECISION
) WITH (tsdb.hypertable);

The tsdb.hypertable parameter is the modern sugar over the classic two-step form CREATE TABLE ...; SELECT create_hypertable('sensor_data', 'time'); — both end in the same C entry point. Inside the extension, that triggers the full creation path from the overview diagram: catalog rows, a time dimension on the time column, and the first chunk.

Then load data and aggregate. The README’s Step 4 enables direct columnstore inserts and generates ~7.8 million rows with generate_series:

SET timescaledb.enable_direct_compress_insert = on;
INSERT INTO sensor_data (time, sensor_id, temperature, humidity, pressure)
SELECT time,
       'sensor_' || ((random() * 9)::int + 1),
       20 + (random() * 15),
       40 + (random() * 30),
       1000 + (random() * 50)
FROM generate_series(NOW() - INTERVAL '90 days', NOW(), INTERVAL '1 seconds') AS time;

Finally, query it the time-series way — bucketing is a first-class SQL function, and the planner knows how to push time predicates down to individual chunks:

SELECT time_bucket('1 hour', time) AS hour,
       sensor_id,
       ROUND(AVG(temperature)::numeric, 2) AS avg_temp
FROM sensor_data
WHERE time > NOW() - INTERVAL '24 hours'
GROUP BY hour, sensor_id
ORDER BY hour DESC, sensor_id
LIMIT 20;

The Detail View: Write Path, Columnstore, Aggregates, Workers

The detail graph separates the sources into eight groups. Follow the write path from partitioning through tuple routing to chunk insert state; follow the read path from the planner hook through hypertable expansion into chunk pruning.

The write path in detail. The executor asks for a routing plan once per statement, then for every row the partitioning functions produce a point; existing chunks are found through the subspace store memo, and a miss calls ts_chunk_create_for_point, which builds a ts_hypercube_add_slice_from_range, L129 hypercube and materializes the child table. Bulk loading via COPY FROM reuses the same machinery from copy_chunk_state_create, L158 instead of spawning a separate code path — a deliberate reuse that keeps COPY semantics identical to INSERT.

The columnstore. When a chunk is compressed, tsl_compress_chunk, L899 wraps the engine-level compress_chunk: rows are sorted by the configured order_by columns, grouped by segment_by columns, and written as compressed columnar batches into a companion table. The settings themselves are catalog objects — ts_compression_settings_get, L400 fetches them per chunk. Setting them up from DDL is tsl_process_compress_table, L1529, and the README’s convert_to_columnstore loop maps to tsl_move_to_columnstore, L1182. Inserts into already-compressed chunks trigger on-demand decompression of the affected batches during routing.

Continuous aggregates. Declaring CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... WITH (timescaledb.continuous) is parsed by tsl_process_continuous_agg_viewstmt, L783, which builds a hidden materialization hypertable. When rows in raw chunks change, continuous_agg_dml_invalidate, L921 appends affected time ranges to a persistent log via invalidation_cagg_log_add_entry, L230. A scheduled job later calls continuous_agg_refresh, which re-aggregates only the invalidated windows — that is what makes refreshes cheap on large datasets. Policies like add_continuous_aggregate_policy, L99 simply register jobs.

Background workers. Policies need a scheduler, and TimescaleDB ships one inside the database. The launcher (ts_bgw_cluster_launcher_main, L860) runs under the postmaster, spawns a per-database scheduler (ts_bgw_scheduler_main, L1028), which polls the jobs catalog and executes due jobs with ts_bgw_job_start, L80. Retention, compression, and continuous-aggregate refresh policies are all just rows in that jobs table, which is why the whole policy system survives restarts with no external daemon.

Honest Limits

  • This tour covers the extension sources, not the storage engine: TimescaleDB inherits all of PostgreSQL’s storage semantics, including vacuum, WAL, and replication behavior, from the core server it runs inside.
  • The README’s performance claims (for example, columnstore compression of “90%+ typical” and sub-100ms skipscan queries) are quoted from its quick start, not independently benchmarked here; your numbers will depend on data shape and hardware.
  • Compression and continuous aggregates live in tsl/ under the Timescale License (the community edition, free to use and self-host, but not open-source-licensed in the Apache sense); the core in src/ and sql/ is Apache 2. The license split is enforced by the cross-module function interface, visible as *_stub fallbacks in src/cross_module_fn.c.
  • The diagrams reflect main at version 2.32.0-dev. The codebase moves quickly — line numbers will drift in future releases, though the module layout has been stable for years.
  • Writing directly into compressed chunks works, but the README recommends the batched convert_to_columnstore flow after ingestion; direct inserts pay a decompression cost on touched batches.

Where to Go Next

If you are evaluating storage for machine-learning workloads, TimescaleDB pairs naturally with the rest of the Postgres ecosystem: dashboards over time-series data are a common Grafana use case, and long-term metric storage is exactly what the PromQL-compatible tooling around Prometheus wants from a remote database. If you are comparing engines, our ClickHouse tour covers the columnar-native alternative with a very different architecture trade-off, and if your AI stack needs embeddings next to your time-series rows, pgvector in the same PostgreSQL instance keeps the operational story to one system. For the source itself, start at github.com/timescale/timescaledb and follow the diagram links into the real code.
entry.summary: An annotated architecture tour of the timescale/timescaledb C codebase: hypertable creation, tuple routing into chunks, the planner hook, columnstore compression, continuous aggregates, and background workers.

entry.title: Typesense Source Tour: How the C++ Search Engine Is Wired, From HTTP to Inverted Index

link.title: Typesense Source Tour: How the C++ Search Engine Is Wired, From HTTP to Inverted Index

entry.content:
Typesense is a compact, open-source search engine written in C++ that has quietly become the default answer for teams that need typo-tolerant, millisecond-latency search without operating a distributed JVM cluster. Its promise, repeated in the project’s own README, is simplicity: a single Docker image, a single API key, and a REST interface that feels more like a document store than a heavyweight enterprise search appliance. That simplicity is real, but it is the product of some very deliberate systems engineering underneath, and the best way to appreciate it is to read the source directly.

This post is a source tour of the typesense/typesense repository at its current default branch, v31. We walked the tree with a parser’s eye, verified every symbol and line number with grep against the working tree, and drew two interactive diagrams: an overview of the major subsystems and a detail view of roughly thirty functions that carry a query from a socket to a scored result. Clicking any node in the SVGs below opens the exact file on GitHub at the v31 branch, so you can follow along without cloning anything.

Three ideas organize everything you will see. First, all primary search structures live in memory while raw JSON documents are persisted to disk through RocksDB. Second, every write travels through a RAFT log so that a cluster of nodes agrees on a single order of operations before anything is indexed. Third, the query path is a stack of small, composable passes: schema validation, filter compilation, token expansion over an adaptive radix tree, posting-list intersection, and a bounded top-K heap that decides what you actually see.

Overview: requests arrive through the h2o-based HTTP layer, writes are funneled through a batched RAFT state machine, and reads hit the per-collection in-memory index backed by an adaptive radix tree and RocksDB.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Endpoint registration happens once at boot in master_server_routes, L22, which binds URIs like /collections/:collection/documents/search to plain C++ handlers in core_api.cpp.
  • The HTTP layer itself is HttpServer::run, L233, an event loop built on the h2o library, which avoids one-thread-per-connection costs and integrates directly with the replication state.
  • Write requests do not index immediately; they are queued by the BatchedIndexer::run, L205 loop, which coalesces concurrent requests into fewer, larger RAFT log entries.
  • Consensus lives in ReplicationState, where ReplicationState::write, L325 proposes entries as leader or redirects to one, and ReplicationState::on_apply, L540 applies committed entries to the collections in log order.
  • The collection registry is CollectionManager; its read entry point CollectionManager::do_search, L3275 parses request parameters and hands off to the named collection.
  • Document ingestion bottoms out in Collection::add, L996, which wraps the batched path, and search orchestration in Collection::search, L3552, which layers curations, synonyms, and grouping on top of the raw engine call.
  • The engine core is Index, entered through Index::run_search, L2492, a long function that sequences filters, facets, sorting, and grouping around the actual candidate search.
  • Underneath, tokens resolve through art_search, L220 against an adaptive radix tree — the data structure that gives Typesense its cheap fuzzy matching — while the Store, L54 wrapper keeps every raw document durable in RocksDB.

Detail view: the same flow with the interesting functions of each layer exposed, from schema coercion in the collection layer down to token expansion and top-K selection inside the index.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s quick start is genuinely one command. Start the server with:

docker run -p 8108:8108 -v/tmp/data:/data typesense/typesense:29.0 --data-dir /data --api-key=Hu52dwsas2AdxdE

Port 8108 serves both the REST API and (over HTTPS in production setups) the health endpoints the client libraries use for retry decisions. Everything else is plain REST, and you can drive it with curl. Create a collection — the schema container — with POST /collections, handled by post_create_collection, L321. A minimal body names the collection, lists its fields with types such as string and int32, and declares a default_sorting_field so the engine has a static score to blend with text relevance.

Add documents with POST /collections/books/documents, one JSON object per request, or stream newline-delimited JSON to /collections/books/documents/import for bulk loads. Each write is authenticated by the API key sent as an X-TYPESENSE-API-KEY header, validated, coerced against the schema you just created, and appended to the RAFT log rather than indexed inline. Search with GET /collections/books/documents/search?q=moby&q_fields=title — the handler is get_search, L639 — and refine with filter_by, facet_by, sort_by, and page/per_page. If you would rather embed search in another language, official clients exist for JavaScript, Python, PHP, Go, Java, C#, and more, each with built-in retry logic that fails reads over to replicas.

One nuance worth knowing before you build: the Docker tag in the README pins a numbered release (29.0 in the current quick start), while the source tree we are touring is the v31 development branch. Behaviors documented for stable releases can trail or lead the branch, so when a snippet from a tutorial does not compile, the first thing to check is which version the tutorial assumed.

Inside the Search Path

The search path is where Typesense spends its engineering budget, and the detail diagram makes the layering visible. After do_search collects parameters, the collection runs the query under a shared read lock in Collection::run_search_with_lock, L4255. The first pass compiles filter_by expressions — country: US AND genre: fiction — into an iterator tree via filter::parse_filter_query, L901; the same subsystem now understands nested and reference fields. A vector clause, if present, is parsed by VectorQueryOps::parse_vector_query_str, L5 and resolves to a kNN search over an embedded HNSW graph.

Then comes text matching. Index::search, L3542 walks the query tokens against each search field, and Index::search_all_candidates, L1801 performs the real work: exact-match lookup, then prefix expansion, then bounded typo tolerance — one character dropped or swapped for short words, two for longer ones — all against the ART tree. Candidates come back as posting-list intersections; scoring blends token matches, token proximity, and the document’s static sorting field, and the winners are kept in a bounded heap (Topster) before facet counting via Index::do_facets, L1526 annotates the final page.

Two result-shaping mechanisms sit above the engine. Curations — the JSON structures parsed by curation_t::parse, L5 — let an operator pin specific documents for a query, hide others, or replace the query entirely; they are evaluated before the engine sees the final query text. Synonyms, managed through SynonymIndex::add_synonym, L133, come in one-way and multi-way flavors and are expanded during token processing, so a search for “sneaker” can transparently include “shoe” results.

The Write Path and Replication

Writes are deliberately slower on the happy path so that reads can be fast and the cluster can stay consistent. Every mutating request — document add, update, delete, collection create, even curation edits — is serialized through the RAFT machinery in raft_server.cpp. The batched indexer exists because high-throughput indexing of individual documents would otherwise produce one consensus round per document; instead, it drains a queue, deduplicates writes that target the same document id, and hands the batch to the leader. Once committed, on_apply replays the entry, and the collection layer performs the in-memory insertion through Index::batch_memory_index after validation in Index::batch_validate_and_preprocess, L466, which also triggers embedding generation for any auto-embedding field.

Durability is split by design: the ART trees, posting lists, and facet stores are rebuilt from the log on restart, while raw documents and collection metadata land in RocksDB through the Store, L54 wrapper. Snapshots bound log growth, and a node joining the cluster can catch up from a peer’s snapshot rather than replaying history from zero. The error style across all of these layers is uniform — nearly every fallible operation returns the Option<T> type from Option, L6, which carries an HTTP-mappable status code alongside the absence of a value, so errors bubble up to the REST layer without exceptions.

If you are comparing engines, this is the axis where Typesense differs most from its neighbors. Elasticsearch trades that consistency machinery for a much broader feature set and a JVM runtime, as we covered in our Elasticsearch tour; Meilisearch makes the opposite bet with a single-node, replication-light design described in our Meilisearch post.

Honest Limits

Everything flattering above comes from the source and the project’s own claims, so here is the other column of the ledger, also from those sources. The benchmark numbers in the README — 250 concurrent queries per second against 3 million Amazon product records on an 8-vCPU, 3-node cluster — are self-reported, on a dataset the authors describe as the largest they could find in the public domain; they explicitly invite larger benchmarks. The “10 billion searches per month” figure is aggregated across Typesense Cloud customers, not a property of the open-source server itself.

The in-memory-first design has a concrete consequence: your working set must fit in RAM, with RocksDB serving as durability rather than as a spilling index. That makes Typesense inexpensive to run at small and medium scale and progressively more deliberate to operate as a corpus grows. Vector search is real in this codebase but is one feature among many rather than a specialty; if your primary workload is dense retrieval over embeddings, a dedicated library will do more for you, which we discuss in the FAISS and Qdrant tours. Finally, the single-master RAFT design means write throughput is bounded by one leader node, and this tour describes the v31 branch — a moving target — so line numbers cited here will drift as the code evolves.

Where It Fits

As a mental model: Typesense is a purpose-built read-mostly search service that keeps its index entirely in curated in-memory structures, keeps its truth in a replicated log, and exposes both through a small REST surface that any web app can call directly. If your problem is site search, autocomplete, instant filters, and typo tolerance on structured data, it is hard to beat on setup cost. If you need heavyweight analytics or a document database with search bolted on, look at Elasticsearch; if you are indexing embeddings for semantic retrieval at scale, start with Qdrant or Usearch and bring Typesense in for the keyword half of a hybrid system.
entry.summary: A guided architecture tour of the Typesense codebase: h2o HTTP layer, RAFT replication, batched writes, ART-backed inverted index, and the full search path.
